# Results — Study 400 (Patent-Intensity)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The **innovation premium**: rank a
fixed large-cap field by **R&D intensity** (R&D expense / revenue — the audited proxy for
patent-and-invention intensity), go **long the most-intensive tertile / short the least-intensive**,
rebalance annually with a one-year reporting lag, and race the spread against SPY and against a
*blind* random long/short of the same field. We split the claim in two: is the innovation spread
**statistically real** (HAC `t ≥ 2`), and is it a tradable *innovation* factor or **sector/style
beta in disguise** that costs and short-borrow erase? Offline & deterministic from the cache; run
`python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Intensity tape | **SEC EDGAR** companyfacts — annual `ResearchAndDevelopmentExpense` / revenue (public, no key) |
| Return tape | yfinance monthly **total return** (auto-adjusted closes, public, no key) |
| Window | **2005-02 → 2026-05** (256 complete months; **21.3** years) |
| Field | **40** long-listed large-caps spanning the R&D spectrum; **39** have an EDGAR intensity series (GS has no R&D line) |
| Intensity proxy | R&D / revenue per fiscal year — **PROXY** for patent-and-invention intensity (no free issued-patent feed) |
| Formation / costs | annual rebalance, **1-year reporting lag** (year-Y book uses fiscal-year-(Y-1) intensity); 10 bps one-way turnover + **100 bps/yr borrow** on the short leg |
| Panel fingerprint | `66d4e99b7bf1` |

> **Scope caveats (named on the Signal axis).** *Proxy* — reported R&D / revenue is the standard
> stand-in for invention intensity (Chan-Lakonishok-Sougiannis 2001), but it is **not** issued
> patents: it misses the *quality* of R&D and treats a bank's absent R&D line as a true ~0 (which is
> economically correct — banks don't patent — but coarse). *Survivorship* — the basket is
> **current-membership projected back** to 2005 (delisted names absent). Its direction is reasoned
> about in writing: **both** the long leg (R&D-heavy tech/pharma) **and** the short leg (R&D-light
> banks/staples/energy) are survivors, so the survivorship tilt is largely **common to both legs**
> of the long/short rather than a clean push on the spread. *One field* — 40 names is a transparent
> slice, not the CRSP universe; the verdict is about *whether the audited-intensity tilt clears the
> bar on a clean tape*, which it does not.

The long (high-intensity) and short (low-intensity) tertiles as of the final rebalance:

- **Long (high R&D / revenue):** ADBE, AMGN, BMY, CSCO, GILD, IBM, INTC, LLY, MRK, ORCL, PFE, QCOM, TXN
- **Short (low R&D / revenue):** AXP, C, COST, DUK, HD, KO, LOW, MCD, MMM, T, USB, VZ, WMT

The split is exactly the intuition — semis, software and pharma on the long side; banks, staples,
retail, utilities and telco on the short side. That is also the first clue it is a **sector/style
axis**, not a patent-specific one.

## The race — high-intensity long, low-intensity short, vs the market

Equal-weight, annually rebalanced; CAGR / annualised Sharpe / max drawdown over the 256 months.

| book | CAGR | Sharpe | max drawdown | mean (ann) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Long — high-intensity (top tertile)** | **13.64%** | 0.94 | −36.9% | +13.95% |
| Short leg — low-intensity (bottom tertile) | 9.71% | 0.72 | −46.1% | +10.35% |
| **Long − short (the innovation spread)** | 2.98% | **0.31** | −26.6% | **+3.60%** |
| S&P 500 (SPY) | 11.11% | 0.78 | −50.8% | +11.70% |
| Long, net of 10 bps turnover | 13.61% | — | — | — |

The long leg out-earns the short leg — the directional claim is *not nothing*. But the Sharpe of the
long-short is **0.31**: a thin, noisy spread, not a crisp factor.

## The Signal-axis test — HAC t-stats

Newey-West HAC t of the monthly spread (the desk's `REAL` needs `t ≥ 2` on the real tape):

| spread | mean | HAC t | n |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| **Long − short (innovation spread)** | **+3.60%/yr** | **1.50** | 256 |
| Long − SPY | +2.25%/yr | 1.21 | 256 |
| Short − SPY | −1.35%/yr | −0.76 | 256 |

The innovation spread is **+3.60%/yr but `t = 1.50` — it does not clear the `t ≥ 2` bar.** The
long-minus-SPY edge is even weaker (t = 1.21), and the short leg merely lags the market (t = −0.76),
so the spread is *mostly* the long leg's mild outperformance, not a clean two-sided premium. Over a
21-year tape, the "innovation premium" is a positive point estimate the null cannot be rejected against.

## Is it the intensity signal, or any split of a mixed field? — the random control

The decisive control. Draw 2,000 *blind* long/shorts (13 names long, 13 short, names chosen at
random, no intensity used) and see where the **intensity** long-short sits in that distribution:

| | annualised long-short spread |
|---|--:|
| **Intensity long-short (this study)** | **+3.60%/yr** |
| Random blind long/short — mean / median of 2,000 draws | +0.08% / +0.05% /yr |
| Random blind long/short — std dev | 1.77%/yr |
| **Intensity percentile in the random distribution** | **97.9** |

This cuts **both** ways, and that is the honest finding. A *random* split of the field earns ~0%/yr
(as it should — no information), so the intensity spread of +3.60%/yr is **not** a generic artefact:
the R&D ranking really does load on a *persistent cross-sectional axis* (it sits at the 97.9th
percentile of blind splits). **But that axis is the well-known growth/tech-vs-value style tilt** —
the long leg *is* semis-software-pharma and the short leg *is* banks-staples-retail — and even this
informative axis fails to clear `t ≥ 2` on its own time series. So the spread is real-as-a-tilt and
**misattributed**: it is style/sector beta wearing a patent costume, not a distinct, significant
innovation alpha.

## Robustness — the spread is fragile to specification

Tighten the long/short fraction from halves to quintiles:

| split | names/leg | long-short | HAC t |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| top/bottom **half** | 20 | +4.12%/yr | **2.18** |
| top/bottom **tertile** (headline) | 13 | +3.60%/yr | **1.50** |
| top/bottom **quartile** | 10 | +3.28%/yr | 1.29 |
| top/bottom **quintile** | 8 | +3.28%/yr | 1.13 |

The spread clears `t = 2` **only** at the coarsest split (halves, where each "leg" is half the whole
field — barely a tilt at all). At every concentrated, tradable split (tertile and tighter) it
**fails**. A signal that is significant only when you barely sort, and insignificant the moment you
actually concentrate on the most-intensive names, is the textbook `WEAK` pattern — significant raw at
one specification, fragile to the obvious robustness check. (The report-lag is not the issue:
lag = 2 gives +3.52%/yr at t = 1.53, essentially identical.)

## Costs + short-borrow — what little there is, erodes

| leg | gross | net (10 bps turnover + 100 bps/yr borrow on the short) |
|---|--:|--:|
| Long-only mean (ann) | +13.95% | +13.61% CAGR (turnover trivial — annual rebalance) |
| **Long-short spread** | **+3.60%/yr (t = 1.50)** | **+2.60%/yr (t = 1.08)** |

Turnover is tiny (annual rebalance of a 13-name book), so cost is not the executioner. But a
long/short **pays borrow to be short** — and a 100 bps/yr borrow fee on the short leg knocks the
already-insignificant +3.60%/yr spread down to **+2.60%/yr at t = 1.08**. You cannot allocate to a
long/short whose net spread is statistically indistinguishable from zero.

## Synthetic positive control — the engine is faithful, the tape is just weak

A deterministic monthly panel (fixed seed, 18 years × 40 names) where the first half are persistently
high-intensity and the second half low, the market beta is common to both legs, and a knob `edge`
plants the *true* annual long-high-minus-short-low premium:

| planted edge | recovered long-short spread | HAC t |
|---|--:|--:|
| **`edge = 0.00`** (no true premium) | −1.34%/yr | **−0.69** |
| **`edge = 0.06`** (large +6%/yr premium) | +4.33%/yr | **+2.23** |

With **no** planted premium the long-short is flat and **insignificant** (t = −0.69 — the harness
does not manufacture a false positive). Only a **large** planted premium (+6%/yr) drives the
recovered spread above `t = 2`. The engine is unbiased — it finds a premium **only** where one is
planted — which is exactly why the real-tape `t = 1.50` reads as *"a real-but-tiny-or-absent edge
seen through a 21-year keyhole,"* not as a hidden bug.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The innovation long-short is positive (**+3.60%/yr**) and loads on a genuine
  cross-sectional axis (97.9th percentile of random splits), and the literature reports an
  R&D-intensity premium. But on this clean 21-year tape it **fails `t ≥ 2`** (HAC **t = 1.50**),
  clears 2 *only* at the barely-sorted "halves" split, and decays at every concentrated split.
  Literature support + a positive-but-insignificant, specification-fragile estimate ⇒ **WEAK**, not
  `REAL`.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Turnover cost is trivial, but the long/short **pays short-borrow**, which
  drops the spread to **+2.60%/yr at t = 1.08** — a net edge indistinguishable from zero. The
  long-only leg beats SPY by only +2.25%/yr (t = 1.21), most of which is the growth/tech tilt you
  could buy more cheaply as a style ETF. There is no significant, borrow-and-cost-surviving edge to
  allocate to.
- **An innovation premium? — MISATTRIBUTED.** The spread is **not** random noise — it is a real,
  persistent *style/sector* axis (R&D-heavy = growth/tech/pharma; R&D-light = value/banks/staples).
  But that makes the "innovation premium" a **relabelled growth-vs-value tilt**, not a distinct,
  patent-specific alpha — and even the tilt does not clear significance. The premium is attributed to
  *invention*; it is really *style beta*.

> **One-line.** Sort large-caps by audited R&D intensity and the high-intensity tertile does beat the
> low-intensity tertile by +3.60%/yr — but at HAC **t = 1.50** that "innovation premium" never clears
> the significance bar (it reaches t = 2 only when you barely sort, and short-borrow drags the net
> spread to t = 1.08), and the spread is really the growth-vs-value style axis wearing a patent
> costume, not a distinct innovation alpha.
